name: Going Live
sub: From paper to real, without dying

lessons.t: Are you ready? The honest metrics

cards.p: Going live is not a feeling — it is a checklist: at least 100 paper trades, positive expectancy across 3 consecutive months, a journal you actually keep, a written strategy with defined A+ setups, and zero revenge-trading incidents in the last month.

Assume your live performance will be WORSE than paper at first — execution hesitation, emotional interference, spread and fees you barely noticed. If your paper edge is thin, real conditions will erase it. You want a margin of safety in the numbers, not a coin flip.

Nobody hands out medals for going live early, and the market will still be here next year. Every month of disciplined paper trading is cheap tuition; every premature live month is expensive tuition for the same lesson. The patient path and the fast path end at the same place — one just costs more.

o: 100+ trades and 3 months of positive expectancy with a journal

quiz.q: Your first live months will likely perform…
o: Worse than paper — plan a margin of safety

cards.p: 1) Is it legal and available in YOUR country — regulation decides everything downstream. 2) Is it liquid in the pairs you trade — thin books eat profits. 3) What are the REAL fees at your size, including funding. 4) What is its security and solvency history — has it ever frozen withdrawals?

An exchange account is a trading venue, not a savings account. Keep only active trading capital there; withdraw profits on a schedule. Enable every security feature — authenticator 2FA, withdrawal allow-lists, anti-phishing codes — before the first deposit, not after the first scare.

A regulated venue in your jurisdiction with modest leverage beats an offshore casino with a 100x button — you now know the 100x button is not the prize, survival is. Deposit small, verify the full loop (deposit → trade → withdraw) with a trivial amount first.

quiz.q: The FIRST question when choosing an exchange is…
o: Is it legal and available in your country

quiz.q: How much should live on an exchange account?
o: Only active trading capital — withdraw the rest

quiz.q: Before real size, you should first…
o: Verify the whole deposit-trade-withdraw loop with a trivial amount

cards.p: Your first live trades should risk about a TENTH of your normal paper risk — small enough that the outcome is irrelevant. The goal is not profit; it is executing your full process (checklist, entry, stop, journal) while real feelings fire for the first time.

Success in week one is: trades that look exactly like your paper trades, just smaller. Same setups, same sizing math, same exits. If your live trading immediately looks different from your paper trading — more trades, bigger size, no stops — stop and go back to paper.

cards.h: Scale by calendar, not by confidence
cards.p: Increase size on a schedule (for example, monthly) and only if the month was disciplined — never mid-week because you feel hot. Feelings of invincibility are a lagging indicator of a winning streak and a leading indicator of the give-back.

o: About a tenth of normal — outcome irrelevant, process everything

quiz.q: Success in your first live week looks like…
o: Trades identical to your paper trades, just smaller
On a schedule, after disciplined months

cards.p: Paper losses are information; real losses are pain. Expect to cut winners earlier, hesitate on entries and widen mental stops — everyone does at first. This is not a character flaw; it is your brain treating money as survival. Naming it is half the fix.

The professional heuristic: if a position affects your sleep, your mood or your relationships, it is too big — regardless of what the risk math allows. Trade a size where you can follow the plan with total indifference to any single outcome. Indifference is the edge.

Under real pressure, your process is what you practised, not what you know. This is why the paper months mattered: checklist, journal, loss limits — drilled until they run on autopilot. When emotions spike, the autopilot flies the plane.

quiz.q: Cutting winners early when going live is…
o: A near-universal first reaction to real money — name it and size down

quiz.q: If a position affects your sleep, it is…
o: Too big, regardless of the math

cards.p: Every lesson in this academy reduces to one sentence: stay in the game. Edges are found, lost and refound; markets change regimes; strategies decay. The trader still standing — capital intact, process intact, curiosity intact — gets every future opportunity for free.

The learning loop never ends: trade the plan, journal everything, review weekly, kill one leak, repeat. Add tools as they earn their place — the calendar for events, funding and OI for positioning, the screener for candidates. Complexity is earned, never bolted on.

cards.h: You now know more than most
cards.p: Leverage math, liquidation mechanics, sizing, R:R, expectancy, tilt control, market structure, positioning data, macro events — this is genuinely more than the majority of people who fund a futures account ever learn. Keep practising it where mistakes are free, and let the levels mark the road ahead.

quiz.q: The one-sentence summary of the entire academy is…
o: Stay in the game — survival gets you every future opportunity
Trade → journal → review → kill one leak → repeat, forever

quiz.q: Complexity in a trading process should be…
o: Earned — each tool must prove its place

try.p: The Academy is done — the practice never is. Keep the streak alive and let the XP levels track the road.
